response.text:
Accrual accounting and cash-basis accounting simply differ in timing. With cash-basis, you record money when it actually moves — you count income when you get paid and count expenses when you pay a bill. With accrual accounting, you record income when you earn it and expenses when you owe them, even if cash hasn’t changed hands yet.

For example: if you deliver work in June but the client pays in July, accrual accounting records the sale in June; cash-basis records it in July. Similarly, if you receive a bill in May for services used in May but pay in June, accrual records the cost in May while cash-basis waits until June.

Accrual gives a clearer view of performance over a period because it matches what happened with when it happened. Cash-basis is simpler and shows actual cash flow. Businesses that need an accurate picture of ongoing activity usually use accrual accounting; smaller operations or personal finances often use cash-basis.
